note: Studies link out-party perceptions, emotions and individual dispositions to partisan dislike. Evidence includes associations and experimental tests of specific mechanisms.
Associations depend on the platform, political content and pattern of exposure. Results differ across media settings.
The strength of partisan identity and the composition of social networks recur across studies. The effects of cross-party contact vary with prior partisan attachment.
Several studies report greater partisan affect around elections. In-group warmth accounts for part of this change, and coalition signals sometimes reduce polarization.
Findings distinguish personal hardship from perceived collective unfairness. Low perceived mobility can condition how people respond to inequality.
